'''Mabel Gweneth Humphreys''' (1911-2006) was a [[Canadian-American]] [[mathematician]] and Professor of Mathematics at [[Randolph-Macon Women's College|Randolph-Macon Woman's College]].<ref name = "ams-profile">{{cite web |url=http://www.ams.org/publications/authors/books/postpub/hmath-34-PioneeringWomen.pdf |title=Supplementary Material for Pioneering Women in American Mathematics: The Pre-1940 PhD's|last1=Green |first1=Judy |last2=Laduke |first2=Jeanne |website=[[American Mathematical Society]] |date=January 15, 2016 |access-date=May 4, 2020}}</ref>
The [[M. Gweneth Humphreys Award]] of the [[Association for Women in Mathematics]] was established in her honor.<ref name="awm"/>

== Education ==
Humphreys attended North Vancouver High School from 1925 to 1928.
She received her Bachelor of Arts with honors in mathematics from the [[University of British Columbia]] in 1932, where she held scholarships for all four years. She studied at [[Smith College]] under [[Susan Miller Rambo]], among others. She earned a master's degree in mathematics in 1933.<ref name="ams-profile"/> She received her Ph.D. in mathematics from the [[University of Chicago]] in 1935. Her dissertation was entitled ''On the Waring Problem with Polynomial Summands'' and her advisor was [[Leonard Eugene Dickson]].
<ref name="ams-profile"/>
<ref name="genealogy">{{cite web |url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=6324 |title=M. Gweneth (Mabel) Humphreys |website=[[Mathematics Genealogy Project]] |access-date=May 4, 2020 }}</ref>

== Career ==
In 1981, Humphreys described her first attempts to find a job after completing her Ph.D.:
{{Blockquote
|text=I had hoped that the University of Chicago would hear about a job for me, but only one came through, and the male candidate who got his thesis at the same time got that job. In the meantime, I had registered at a teacher’s agency in downtown Chicago, and many cards came in for the sum of something like $900, and you taught all the mathematics in the four years, and you were dean of women, or all of mathematics and coach some sport. I said to myself I wasn’t going to do this; I was going to stick around in Chicago and wait tables somewhere and study more mathematics. After awhile a card came through from Kansas, a woman’s college, and they needed a woman with a Ph.D. in either mathematics or physics to teach both. This was a substitute position, which was vacant because Sr. Helen Sullivan ... was ill. I took that and taught there for that one year. I was very busy I must say, but it was a great apprenticeship. I enjoyed it very much.
|author=Mabel Gweneth Humphreys
(1981)<ref name="ams-profile"/>
}}

From 1935 to 1936, Humphreys was an instructor of mathematics and [[physics]] at [[Mount St. Scholastica College]]. She began teaching at [[H. Sophie Newcomb Memorial College]] in 1936 and was promoted to [[assistant professor]] in 1941. She was also an assistant professor at [[Barnard College]] in the summer of 1944, and an assistant professor at [[Tulane University]] in the summer of 1946.<ref name="ams-profile"/>

In 1949, Humphreys became an [[associate professor]] of mathematics at Randolph-Macon Woman's College in [[Lynchburg, Virginia]].<ref name="SunDial19490519">{{cite journal |title=New Members To Join Faculty |journal=Sun Dial |date=19 May 1949 |volume=35 |issue=28 |page=3 |url=https://virginiachronicle.com/?a=d&d=SDI19490519.1.3 |access-date=4 April 2025}}</ref> After one year at Randolph-Macon, she was named [[Gillie Larew|Gillie A. Larew]] Professor and head of the mathematics department.<ref name="SunDial195006002">{{cite journal |title=Dr. Jack States Faculty Changes |journal=Sun Dial |date=2 June 1950 |volume=36 |issue=29 |page=1 |url=https://virginiachronicle.com/?a=d&d=SDI19500602.1.1 |access-date=4 April 2025}}</ref> She was head of the department until 1979. For the 1955-1956 academic year, Humphreys went on sabbatical leave to the University of British Columbia (UBC). During this time, she visited undergraduate mathematics programs at several colleges and universities to examine their methods. From 1962 to 1963, she was a [[visiting professor]] at UBC as a [[National Science Foundation]] (NSF) faculty fellow.<ref name="ams-profile"/><ref name="SunDial19620201">{{cite journal |title=Math Department Head Accepts NSF Fellowship |journal=Sun Dial |date=1 February 1962 |volume=48 |issue=11 |page=3 |url=https://virginiachronicle.com/?a=d&d=SDI19620201.1.3 |access-date=4 April 2025}}</ref>

In the summers, Humphreys taught high school teachers at NSF summer institutes.<ref name="SunDial19620201"></ref>
From 1965 to 1969, Humphreys worked for the [[Educational Testing Service]].
She was also a consultant in 1975 for the [[American Council on Education]] regarding mathematics course credit given by nonacademic organizations.
Humphreys was an active member of the [[Mathematical Association of America]] at both the sectional and national levels.<ref name="ams-profile"/>

== Awards and legacy ==
Humphreys earned the [[Governor General's Academic Medal#Categories|Governor General's Gold Medal]] in 1932, which was awarded to the college student with the highest grade point average in Canada.<ref name="ams-profile"/>

The [[M. Gweneth Humphreys Award]] of the [[Association for Women in Mathematics]] is named in her honor. Each year, this award is presented to a mathematics educator who has encouraged women undergraduates to pursue mathematical careers.<ref name="awm">{{cite web |url=https://awm-math.org/awards/humphreys-award/ |title=Gweneth Humphreys Awards |access-date=May 4, 2020 |website=[[Association for Women in Mathematics]]}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Humphreys was born on October 22, 1911 in [[South Vancouver, British Columbia]]. Her mother, Mabel Jane Thomas (1885-1963), was born in [[London, England]], and worked as a dressmaker and a florist.
Her father was Richard Humphreys (1880-1969), a [[machinist]] who was born in [[Pwllheli]], Wales. Her parents were married in 1910, and Humphreys was their only child.<ref name="ams-profile"/> In 1941, Humphreys became a naturalized [[U.S. citizen]].<ref name="ams-profile"/>

Humphreys' hobbies included gardening and reading.
She was an active member of the [[Appalachian Trail Conservancy#Affiliated trail maintenance clubs|Natural Bridge Appalachian Trail Club]].
She lived in [[Lynchburg, Virginia]], through her retirement in 1980 until her death on October 6, 2006.<ref name="ams-profile"/>
